# How This Book Is Written {.unnumbered}

Writing a book in the open is an intentional act of vulnerability. I am composing this synthesis during an academic sabbatical at Harvard University while spending dedicated time at ETH Zürich, with the goal of bringing a fully polished volume to completion by the end of 2027. Sharing early drafts with colleagues, students, and the broader architecture community forces every idea to defend itself in public long before the ink is dry. Working with generative AI systems every day quickly exposes both their practical utility and their failure modes.

The basis for this book grew out of our initial paper on Architecture 2.0 [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. Bringing computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation together into a coherent framework required years of work across three distinct communities. Each of these fields operates under different physical constraints and evidence standards, and bridging them demands far more than a clever prompt.

To write this book, I apply the exact pedagogical principles we teach inside it, using a backward-design methodology refined through [Harvard's Learning Incubator (LInc)](https://linc.seas.harvard.edu/) program [@WigginsMcTighe2005BackwardDesign]. Every chapter starts by defining the core architectural questions, physical trade-offs, and lasting principles; I establish the evidence requirements next and draft the explanatory prose last.

I treat generative models not as co-authors, but as an expansive information vault. Much like web search engines transformed research two decades ago, generative systems allow me to probe creative design alternatives, explore interdisciplinary literature, and surface historical connections efficiently. Yet an information vault has no architectural taste, no physical intuition, and no engineering accountability. Generative models can synthesize options, but they cannot take responsibility for a tapeout decision or defend an architectural choice against real-world constraints.

To maintain technical rigor, I built an authoring pipeline structured around specialized review roles. Simulated learner panels test pedagogical clarity. Senior architect panels push on technical bounds and physical reality. Systems panels inspect tool interfaces and synthesis assumptions. Citation auditors trace claims, benchmark figures, and equations back to primary literature. As shown in @fig-author-ai-workflow, these review roles feed directly into an automated build harness that compiles the manuscript, validates references, and verifies formatting.

![**The AI-assisted authoring engine operates as an out-of-order multi-agent design loop.** Backward design establishes intent first. The generation swarm communicates across a shared inter-agent bus to propose drafts, while simulated review panels supply critique. The human author in the central hub functions with in-order commit authority over what reaches the deterministic validation harness. System architects will recognize a structural parallelism to a modern out-of-order CPU datapath: Stage 1 acts as frontend fetch and decode, the agent swarms act as parallel execution units, and the central author hub acts as the reorder buffer and commit stage holding 100% retirement authority.](images/fig-author-ai-workflow.svg){#fig-author-ai-workflow width="100%" fig-alt="Architecture diagram showing Stage 1 Backward Design, Stage 2 Human-in-the-Loop Core and Simulated Agent Review Panels, Stage 3 Validation Harness."}

This pipeline quickly taught me that generation velocity is not synthesis quality. In an early draft, an agent swarm produced thirty pages of fluent prose on hardware-software co-design in under two minutes. On close inspection, however, the text subtly blurred the line between cycle-accurate simulation and physical signoff gates, offering smooth generalities where hard engineering trade-offs belonged. Rebuilding that chapter required hours of pruning back to first principles. As architects and authors, our primary contribution is not generating text; it is exercising the diagnostic taste and non-negotiable commit authority required to reject plausible slop.

Developing the manuscript alongside runnable reference code keeps these principles grounded in executable reality. While the manuscript and reference code are developed in the open, I keep the internal prompt orchestrations, subagent configurations, and rule files private. Just as a chip design team open-sources reference RTL while guarding internal PDK flows and physical design scripts, the engineering value lies in how the machinery is governed to enforce rigor.

Writing is how I test whether I truly understand a subject well enough to teach it. When an explanation cannot survive a reader's questions, the synthesis is not finished. This remains a working manuscript, and I welcome your feedback. If you spot a flaw, an imprecise claim, or a trade-off that needs a harder test, please reach out to me directly.

Vijay Janapa Reddi
*Harvard University / ETH Zürich*
